say: Today you are angle and line detectives. Detectives do not guess: they check every clue with a tool. Our tool is a right-angle checker that you make yourself from any scrap of paper.
By the end you will be able to find every angle in a picture without missing one, and spot lines that never meet.
Look at each clock. Make the two hands with your arms. Is the angle a right angle, like the corner of a book? Smaller? Or bigger?
I will fold a torn piece of paper with wiggly edges, twice. Will the corner I make be a right angle, even though the paper is wiggly? Thumbs up for yes, down for no.
stuck: Stuck folding: fold once to make a straight edge, then fold that edge onto itself so the two halves line up exactly.
Not sure if it is a right angle: put the corner of your checker into the angle. If both arms line up with the edges, it is a right angle.
Ready for more: find an angle that is exactly 2 right angles. (A straight line!)

say: “Here are 4 lines from one point. I count the small angles first: 3. Then the angles made of 2 small ones: 2. Then 3 small ones: 1. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. I go in order so I never miss one.”
“2 lines make 1 angle, 3 lines make 3, 4 lines make 6. The jumps are 2, 3, 4… so the next jump is 5. I can predict without drawing.”
“To count right angles in a picture I visit every point where lines meet, one by one, and write how many right angles are at each point. Then I add.”

do: Ask: “Did you check that corner with your checker, or did you guess?”
Ask: “Which points have you visited? Which are left?”
Ask: “Do these two lines ever meet if we make them longer?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Use your right-angle checker on every corner.”
Hint 2: “Count the small angles first, then the bigger ones made of small ones.”
Hint 3: “Make a list of every pair of lines and test each pair.”

say: “Mei says an angle with longer arms is bigger. Do you agree? How can you test it?”
“How did you make sure you did not miss any angles?”
ask: “Mei says an angle with longer arms is bigger. Do you agree? How can you test it?”

No. The size of an angle is how far the arms open (how much one arm turns to reach the other). Draw two angles that open the same amount, one with long arms and one with short arms: the checker fits both the same way. To miss none, count in order: small angles first, or visit every meeting point.

say: “You checked with a tool, counted in order and found a pattern. That is how real detectives work. Well done!”

p3l8-title.note: Objective: Compare angles with a right angle using a folded-paper checker, count the angles at a point and the right angles in shapes and figures in an organised way, find a pattern in the counts, and find and draw perpendicular and parallel lines. Heuristics taught today: (1) count in an organised way (small angles first; visit every corner or meeting point), (2) look for a pattern. Materials: scrap paper to fold a right-angle checker (one per child), a ruler, mini whiteboards, square grid paper. Online: each child folds a checker on camera and does the right-angle hunt at home; annotate the grid slides with the pen tool. Print the workbook before the lesson. Pairs work in one breakout room for 10 minutes, then return for the check slide. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 4.5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 4.5 to 7.5 (two rounds) and three quick questions 7.5 to 10.5, explore 10.5 to 24 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 24 to 34.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 34.5 to 39.5, worksheet 39.5 to 70.5 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 67.5 everyone chooses), talk time 70.5 to 78.5 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 78.5 to 84.5, look back 84.5 to 87.5, stamp and close 87.5 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it.

p3l8-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 4.5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "say it" ONCE for both: children say both answers together on three (about 30 seconds); nothing is held up to the camera. SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and say them together on three (once for both puzzles); nothing is held up to the camera. No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): L and H have square corners; H has two lines that never meet. Listen for: L and H have square corners; O has none. The two upright lines of H stay the same distance apart. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): 1 right angle each. Listen for: Only the corner that was not cut is still a right angle. The corners that were cut are split into two smaller angles. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l8-warm1.note: Minutes 4.5 to 7.5. Everyone stands. Play TWO rounds of three clocks (the first three, then the last three). For each clock children make the hands with their arms (one arm straight up for the minute hand at 12, the other arm for the hour hand), then say "right angle", "smaller" or "bigger". Click to show the answer (clicks go clock by clock). Answers: 3 o’clock right angle; 1 o’clock smaller; 5 o’clock bigger; 9 o’clock right angle; 10 o’clock smaller; 4 o’clock bigger. Ask: "Why are 3 o’clock and 9 o’clock both right angles?" (The hour hand is a quarter of the way round, one way or the other.) "Which is bigger: 4 o’clock or 5 o’clock?" (5). Watch for children who think 9 o’clock is bigger because 9 is a bigger number.

p3l8-warm2.note: Minutes 7.5 to 10.5. Whiteboards, then click. Answers: 1) 4 2) 6 3) L or T (V has 2 lines that meet, but not at a right angle) Three quick questions only. The fourth (do the two long edges of a ruler ever meet? No: they stay the same distance apart all the way along; lines like that are called parallel) is on the take-home box of the Go further page in the workbook; we meet parallel lines in the worksheet.

p3l8-explore1.note: Minutes 10.5 to 20. Predict first: "If I fold a torn, wiggly piece of paper twice, will the corner be a right angle?" Then everyone folds a checker (the tutor shows a model on the slide): folding the checker is the Explore task, and children keep it for Q1 of the worksheet, so Q1 only has to sort. Fold twice and hunt (about 6 minutes of pair work): children hunt round the room (or at home) and record on a whiteboard: 3 right angles, 1 smaller, 1 bigger. Hints: "Put the corner of the checker into the angle. Do both arms line up?" "If one arm is hidden under the checker, the angle is smaller." Ready for more: find an angle that is exactly 2 right angles (a straight line). GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): Fold your corner in half again. Smaller or bigger than a right angle? Find two. Answer: Smaller than a right angle: it is half of a right angle, so two of them make one right angle. It appears at the corner of a set square, or when a square is cut along its diagonal. Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l8-explore2.note: Minutes 20 to 24. Gather the group. Answers: 1) The first fold makes a straight line (a straight angle). Folding that line exactly onto itself cuts the straight angle into 2 equal parts, and each part is a right angle. The wiggly edges do not matter. 2) No. The size of an angle is how far the arms open (how much one arm turns to reach the other), not how long the arms are. Show two pencils opened the same amount, then slide one pencil out: the angle does not change. 3) For example a door opened wide, an open laptop, a clock at 5 o’clock, the corners of a hexagon tile.

p3l8-teach1.note: Teach. Ask first: "Which angle is bigger?" Many children choose P because its arms are long. Do not correct yet. Click 1: the checker on P (one arm along the bottom arm): the other arm is hidden under the checker, so P is smaller than a right angle. Click 2: the checker on Q: the other arm is outside, so Q is bigger than a right angle. Click 3: the conclusion. Think-aloud: "An angle shows how much one arm turns to reach the other. Long arms or short arms, the turn is the same. To compare, I always line the checker up with one arm and look where the other arm goes."

p3l8-teach2.note: Ask first: "How many corners? How many right angles inside?" Many children say 6 and 6. Click 1: the start dot and the 5 square corners, checked one by one. Click 2: the dent corner: put the checker INSIDE the shape at that corner: the inside angle is much bigger (it goes three-quarters of the way round). Click 3: the answer. Think-aloud: "I put a dot where I start so I visit every corner once. I check each one: is the inside a right angle? A dent corner points into the shape, so inside it is bigger." Parallel example: the worksheet shapes are different.

p3l8-we2.note: Click through. Think-aloud: "If I look at the whole picture I will lose count. So I make a list of the meeting points and visit them one by one. At a corner, 1 right angle. Where the middle line meets the top, there is a right angle on its left and one on its right: 2." Ask: "At the middle of the top, is there an angle made of both right angles together?" (That is a straight line, 2 right angles: we do not count it as a right angle.) Parallel example: the worksheet window has two lines.

p3l8-try2.note: Whiteboards, then click. a) 4: one in each quarter where the lines cross. b) 6: the T has 8 corners; the 2 corners under the arms are dents, bigger than a right angle inside. c) 4: the middle line meets each upright line in its middle, making 2 right angles at each meeting point. The ends of the lines are not corners.

p3l8-teach3.note: Teach the two words with arms: one arm up, one arm out sideways: perpendicular. Both arms up: parallel. On the parallel picture, the dotted ends show the lines carrying on: they never meet. Then the F: click through. Think-aloud: "To find every pair I make a list: a with b, a with c, b with c. That is all of them. Then I test each pair: do they meet at a right angle? Are they always the same distance apart?" Parallel example: the worksheet asks about E.

p3l8-key.note: Say the key ideas together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Thinking a turned right angle (Q1 a) is not a right angle, or that longer arms make a bigger angle (Q1 d and f). Use the checker every time. (2) Counting every corner as a right angle in Q2: dent corners are bigger inside. The roof top of the house IS a right angle: check it. (3) Counting angles at random in Q3: count by size. (4) In Q6, counting only the 4 small squares' corners and missing angles, or counting a straight line as a right angle.

p3l8-break.note: Five minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p3l8-we1.note: Teach heuristic 1: count in an organised way. Ask first: "How many angles?" Most children say 3. Click through the sizes. Think-aloud: "There are 3 small angles between neighbouring lines. But two small angles side by side also make an angle: the first two together, the last two together: 2. And all three together make 1 big angle. I count by size, smallest first, so I never miss one or count one twice: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6." This is a parallel example: the worksheet has 6 lines.

p3l8-ws1.note: Minutes 41 to 56. Say first: "Use the right-angle checker you folded in Explore; Q1 only asks you to sort." Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. Q3(b) (8 lines, look for a pattern) is a take-home question (starred in the workbook). Q1: insist on the checker, especially for a (turned) and d (short arm). Q2: the house roof top is a right angle; let them discover it with the checker. Q3: "How many small angles are there? Now 2 together?" PAGE 1 CLOCK (41 to 56): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 11.5 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l8-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: a is a right angle that is turned; d is a right angle with one short arm; f has long arms but is smaller. Q2: A has 12 corners but 4 are dents; B has 8 corners with 2 dents; C: the 2 bottom corners and the roof top (the corners where the walls meet the roof are bigger); D: the 2 left corners. Q3: 6 lines make 5 small angles. The pattern of jumps: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l8-teachgrid.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 asks for parallel and perpendicular lines on a grid; these lines use different steps). Click 1: count the steps along PQ. Click 2: from R, copy the same steps: the new line never meets PQ. Click 3: swap 3 and 1 and turn: 1 right and 3 down. Put a paper checker on S to show the right angle. Think-aloud: "Parallel lines go the same way, so they have the same steps. For perpendicular, I swap the two numbers and turn the line round." Watch for children who swap but do not turn (1 right, 3 up): check it with the checker, it is not a right angle.

p3l8-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Q4b: "List the pairs first." Q6 is if time: "Which points have you visited?"

p3l8-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q4: in Z and N the slanted line is not at a right angle to the others. Q4b: E has an upright line and 3 short lines: the 3 short lines make 3 parallel pairs, and each one with the upright line is a perpendicular pair. Q5: check each drawn line with the checker. Q6: 4 corners × 1 = 4; 4 points where the lines meet the sides × 2 = 8; the middle crossing has 4. 4 + 8 + 4 = 16. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l8-stretch.note: SUPPORT FOR TAKE-HOME Q3(b) (8 lines at a point; this replaces the old try-it slide), for a child who chooses it: draw the lines on a whiteboard and count small angles first. 2 lines make 1 angle, 3 lines make 3, 4 lines make 6: the jumps are +2, +3, so the next is +4. A new line makes a new angle with every line already there, which is why the jump grows by 1. Do not give the answer for 8 lines (28); it is also in the Investigation. For children who choose Think harder. Answers: 1) For example, on a grid with the bottom-left corner at (0, 0): corners at 0 across 0 up, 4 across 0 up, 3 across 2 up, 0 across 3 up. Only the bottom-left corner is a right angle (check the other three with the checker). 2) No. If two corners on the bottom side were right angles, both other sides would go straight up and be parallel, so they would never meet to close the triangle. 3) 3 pairs: the two upright lines are parallel; the line across is perpendicular to each upright line. So 1 pair of parallel lines and 2 pairs of perpendicular lines.

p3l8-challenge.note: Use as a pair challenge or in talk time. Ask for the reason every time. Answers: 1) 24 (4 at the corners; each of the 5 lines makes 2 right angles at the top and 2 at the bottom: 4 + 5 × 4 = 24). 2) No. The most is 5, for example an L shape. More are in the question bank.

p3l8-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? Which heuristic could help: count in order, or look for a pattern (try 1 square, 2 squares, 3 squares first)? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p3l8-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: when a problem is big, try smaller ones and look for a pattern: 4, 8, 12 … goes up by 4 because each new line meets the top and the bottom, with 2 right angles at each. Q2: let children try to draw 6 square corners along the grid lines: they always get a dent. A proof is not expected: children see that 6 square corners always give a dent, and the best they can draw is the L shape with 5 square corners and 1 dent.

p3l8-talk.note: Minutes 70.5 to 78.5. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: No. The size of an angle is how far the arms open. Test: draw the same angle twice, once with long arms and once with short arms, and put the checker on both: it fits the same way. Or open two pencils the same amount, then slide one out. Follow-up: "How did you make sure you did not miss any angles?" (Count small ones first; visit every meeting point.) TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l8-exit.note: Minutes 78.5 to 84.5. Answer: F and H. F: the top and middle lines are parallel, and each meets the upright line at a right angle. H: the two upright lines are parallel, and the middle line is perpendicular to both. V: two lines that meet, not at a right angle. Z: the top and bottom are parallel, but the slanted line is not perpendicular to them. Extension: how many right angles are in a square drawn as a noughts-and-crosses grid? (36) Answers stay on the child’s own paper and are ticked against the answer slide. Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l8-reflect.note: Minutes 84.5 to 87.5. Look back: short and safe. SAY: "Turn to the last page of today and find Look back. Tick or write one thing for each line. There are no right answers, and you may pass on any line." Give the children a full 2 minutes, then a short share (the slide has 3 minutes). The page is never collected, marked or read out in front of the group. Children keep their page. The tutor does not see the page, so say: "If something is still puzzling you, you can show this page to a grown-up at home, or tell me at the start of next lesson." At the start of the next lesson, in the open session, invite anyone who would like another look at a puzzle (volunteers only, by hand signal or in the chat; never a private message). Invite volunteers only (one or two) to share something they did well, or what helped. Praise the strategy ("you drew it and that got you unstuck"), not the speed or the answer. Then stamp the journal and close (minutes 87.5 to 90).
